ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Circle $C_0$ has radius $1$, and the point $A_0$ is a point on the circle. Circle $C_1$ has radius $r<1$ and is internally tangent to $C_0$ at point $A_0$. Point $A_1$ lies on circle $C_1$ so that $A_1$ is located $90^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from $A_0$ on $C_1$. Circle $C_2$ has radius $r^2$ and is internally tangent to $C_1$ at point $A_1$. In this way a sequence of circles $C_1,C_2,C_3,...$ and a sequence of points on the circles $A_1,A_2,A_3,...$ are constructed, where circle $C_n$ has radius $r^n$ and is internally tangent to circle $C_{n-1}$ at point $A_{n-1}$, and point $A_n$ lies on $C_n$ $90^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from point $A_{n-1}$, as shown in the figure below. There is one point $B$ inside all of these circles. When $r=\frac{11}{60}$, the distance from the center of $C_0$ to $B$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a largest circle, with point A0 marked on the circumference on the right side; a smaller circle is internally tangent to the large circle at A0. A1 is marked above the smaller circle, in a position equivalent to rotating a quarter turn counterclockwise from A0 along this small circle. A further inward circle is internally tangent near A1, and A2 is marked on the left side, also showing the positional relationship of continuing to rotate 90° counterclockwise. Therefore the image is consistent with the continuous internal tangency and each counterclockwise 90° rotation in the problem statement. Reasoning: Put the center of C0 at the origin of the complex plane, and let the coordinate of A0 be 1. The radius of C0 is 1, and the radius of Cn is r^n. Suppose the direction from the center of C_{k-1} to the tangency point A_{k-1} is i^{k-1}; because the position of the point rotates 90° counterclockwise at each step, the direction is multiplied by i each time. C_k and C_{k-1} are internally tangent at A_{k-1}, so the center of C_k, relative to the center of C_{k-1}, moves in the direction i^{k-1} by a distance r^{k-1}-r^k=(1-r)r^{k-1}. Therefore the coordinate of the nth center is (1-r) sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (ri)^k. Since r<1, the circle radii tend to 0, and the unique point B contained in all the circles is the limit of the centers: z_B=(1-r) sum_{k=0}^∞ (ri)^k=(1-r)/(1-ri). So the distance from B to the center of C0 is |z_B|=(1-r)/|1-ri|=(1-r)/sqrt(1+r^2). Substitute r=11/60: |z_B|=(49/60)/sqrt(1+121/3600) =(49/60)/sqrt(3721/3600) =(49/60)/(61/60) =49/61. Therefore m=49, n=61, m+n=110.

|z_B|=(49/60)/sqrt(1+121/3600)
=(49/60)/sqrt(3721/3600)

method.method_draft: Use a self-similarity/fixed-point equation. First observe from the image that after C1, the nested pattern inside C1 has the same shape as the original pattern, but scaled down and rotated 90 degrees counterclockwise: A0 is the right tangency point, A1 is the top point of C1, and the next smaller circle continues from there. From the text, C1 has radius r and its center lies on the radius from the center of C0 to A0, at distance 1-r from the center of C0. Set the center of C0 at the origin and let z be the complex vector from the center of C0 to B, with A0 in the positive real direction. Then the vector from the center of C1 to B must be r times the original vector rotated by 90 degrees, i.e. r i z. Therefore z=(1-r)+ri z. Solve z=(1-r)/(1-ri). The required distance is |z|=(1-r)/sqrt(1+r^2). With r=11/60, this is 49/61, so m+n=49+61=110.

raw_record.original_question: Circle $C_0$ has radius $1$, and the point $A_0$ is a point on the circle. Circle $C_1$ has radius $r<1$ and is internally tangent to $C_0$ at point $A_0$. Point $A_1$ lies on circle $C_1$ so that $A_1$ is located $90^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from $A_0$ on $C_1$. Circle $C_2$ has radius $r^2$ and is internally tangent to $C_1$ at point $A_1$. In this way a sequence of circles $C_1,C_2,C_3,\ldots$ and a sequence of points on the circles $A_1,A_2,A_3,\ldots$ are constructed, where circle $C_n$ has radius $r^n$ and is internally tangent to circle $C_{n-1}$ at point $A_{n-1}$, and point $A_n$ lies on $C_n$ $90^{\circ}$ counterclockwise from point $A_{n-1}$, as shown in the figure. There is one point $B$ inside all of these circles. When $r=\frac{11}{60}$, the distance from the center of $C_0$ to $B$ is $\frac{m}{n}$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure there is a largest circle, with point A0 marked on the circumference on the right side; a smaller circle is internally tangent to the large circle at A0. A1 is marked above the smaller circle, in a position equivalent to rotating a quarter turn counterclockwise from A0 along this small circle. A further inward circle is internally tangent near A1, and A2 is marked on the left side, also showing the positional relationship of continuing to rotate 90° counterclockwise. Therefore the image is consistent with the continuous internal tangency and each counterclockwise 90° rotation in the problem statement.

Reasoning: Put the center of C0 at the origin of the complex plane, and let the coordinate of A0 be 1. The radius of C0 is 1, and the radius of Cn is r^n. Suppose the direction from the center of C_{k-1} to the tangency point A_{k-1} is i^{k-1}; because the position of the point rotates 90° counterclockwise at each step, the direction is multiplied by i each time.

C_k and C_{k-1} are internally tangent at A_{k-1}, so the center of C_k, relative to the center of C_{k-1}, moves in the direction i^{k-1} by a distance r^{k-1}-r^k=(1-r)r^{k-1}. Therefore the coordinate of the nth center is
(1-r) sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (ri)^k.

Since r<1, the circle radii tend to 0, and the unique point B contained in all the circles is the limit of the centers:
z_B=(1-r) sum_{k=0}^∞ (ri)^k=(1-r)/(1-ri).

So the distance from B to the center of C0 is
|z_B|=(1-r)/|1-ri|=(1-r)/sqrt(1+r^2).

Substitute r=11/60:
|z_B|=(49/60)/sqrt(1+121/3600)
=(49/60)/sqrt(3721/3600)
=(49/60)/(61/60)
=49/61.

Therefore m=49, n=61, m+n=110.
